title: The 5 Big Ideas of Literature
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles proposes five unifying principles to organize an English literature curriculum: religion, class, the role of women, education, and science. His argument is that without such principles each text looks random to students, linked at best by theme, and a theme-based curriculum is merely decoration. The Big Ideas let teachers show that every text responds to the social issues of its era, and each is illustrated with a worked reading of Macbeth. He adds that the five ideas are interrelated and still relevant to today's texts and news, giving students a way to understand chronology and their own culture. The piece is an extract from his book and ends with promotional links.
points: A theme-based curriculum is surface decoration, while recurring underlying principles give students a coherent way to connect texts.
Religion, class, women, education and science are proposed as five archetypal concerns found in nearly every text in the school canon.
Even texts that exclude women or seem unscientific can be read through these lenses, since exclusion and absence themselves carry meaning.
Each idea is shown through a Macbeth reading, giving teachers a model for classroom application.
The Big Ideas are interrelated and let students trace how literature responds to changing societies over time.
quotes: Without these, I believe that each text we study will appear random to the students who study them, or at best be linked by theme. To use an analogy, if literature is like a house, themes are just how we decorate the rooms.

A theme based curriculum is ephemeral and surface level, unless we have principles which underpin literature, principles which will be relevant to every theme. These 5 Big Ideas of literature are what I believe to be the underlying principles.

All of the literature we study in schools, from the Greek myths and beyond, are a response to the cultural and social issues of the day. It makes sense to think about archetypal issues which recur, in every era.

This can be, but doesn’t have to be, a feminist reading of texts. Because women have been denied equality for all but the most recent years of our history, every text we study can appropriately be viewed through this lens.

We can also see that all these Big Ideas are all interrelated. A character’s social status is often dependent on their gender, or their education. A woman’s role is often determined by Christian expectations of morality, or a Christian interpretation of Original Sin.

If we link the Big Ideas to every text we study, all our students will understand these unifying principles. They will understand that texts respond to the societies and eras in which they were written.
